auto-b1-what-agents-automations-are.q: A task involves copying new form responses into a spreadsheet with no judgment calls involved. What kind of solution does this call for?
options: A full autonomous AI agent with tool access
A classic trigger-action automation, since it's pure mechanical data transfer with no AI judgment step
An AI-in-the-loop workflow with a summarization step
A custom-built application from scratch
auto-b1-what-agents-automations-are.why: Mechanical-only tasks — moving data with no judgment involved — usually need a classic automation, not an agent; jumping straight to an AI agent for pure data transfer just adds cost and failure points.

auto-b1-what-agents-automations-are.q: You're picking your first automation project from five candidate tasks. Which combination of traits should you prioritize?
options: The most annoying task on the list, regardless of frequency or risk
The task that touches customer-facing communication, since automating that shows the most value
A task with high frequency, real time cost, and low risk if it makes an occasional mistake
The most technically ambitious task to prove the automation platform's capability
auto-b1-what-agents-automations-are.why: The scoring framework ranks candidates on frequency, time cost, and risk tolerance — a good first project is low-risk and high-frequency to build confidence, not the most ambitious or most annoying task.

auto-b1-what-agents-automations-are.q: One of your five candidate tasks is "processing refund requests over $500." Why might this be a poor choice for your very first automation?
options: It doesn't repeat often enough to be worth automating
It touches money and customer-facing outcomes, which is risky before you've built confidence with something lower-stakes
Refund processing can't be automated with any AI tool
It requires an MCP connector that doesn't exist yet
auto-b1-what-agents-automations-are.why: Picking a task that touches money, legal commitments, or customer-facing communication as the very first automation, before building confidence with something lower-stakes, is a listed common mistake.

auto-b2-map-a-process-to-automate.q: You describe your process to an AI as "customer emails come in, we respond." What's wrong with feeding this into the process-mapping prompt?
options: It's fine — the AI will infer all the missing systems and steps automatically
It's too vague; without naming actual systems and step order, the resulting map will be equally vague and unusable
It should be described in a spreadsheet instead of a prompt
The AI will reject the prompt outright for being too short
auto-b2-map-a-process-to-automate.why: Describing the process too vaguely instead of naming the actual systems and order of steps is a listed common mistake — vague input produces a vague, unusable map.

auto-b2-map-a-process-to-automate.q: While mapping an overdue-invoice process, you're tempted to skip documenting rare edge cases like partial payments because "they're rare." What does the lesson say about this?
options: Skipping rare edge cases is fine since automations only need to handle the common path
Rare cases are exactly what breaks unattended automations in production, so they should be documented, not skipped
Edge cases should only be documented after the automation has already failed once
Edge cases are only relevant for AI-in-the-loop automations, not classic ones
auto-b2-map-a-process-to-automate.why: Skipping edge cases because 'they're rare' is a listed common mistake — rare cases are precisely what breaks unattended automations once they're live.

auto-b2-map-a-process-to-automate.q: Why does the process-mapping prompt explicitly instruct the AI to use only the information given and not invent tools or steps?
options: To keep the prompt shorter
To stop the AI from hallucinating parts of the process it wasn't told about, keeping the map accurate to your real workflow
Because inventing steps would violate the automation platform's terms of service
Because AI models can't name specific software tools
auto-b2-map-a-process-to-automate.why: The anti-hallucination instruction stops the AI from inventing tools, systems, or steps you didn't mention, which is essential since the map needs to reflect your actual process, not a plausible-sounding guess.

auto-b3-mcp-explained.q: You connect Claude to your company's Notion via MCP and later want to use the same server in ChatGPT. What does the lesson say about this?
options: You'd need to build a completely separate integration for ChatGPT
Because MCP is a shared standard, the same server works unmodified across MCP-compatible tools like Claude, ChatGPT, or others
MCP servers are proprietary to whichever AI vendor built them
You'd need to re-authenticate but the server itself needs no changes... this option is intentionally close to correct but wrong on requiring re-integration
auto-b3-mcp-explained.why: MCP is an open, shared standard — connecting one server to Claude means the same server works, unmodified, in ChatGPT or another MCP-compatible tool, without learning a new integration per product.

auto-b3-mcp-explained.q: After connecting an MCP server, a colleague assumes the AI now has full access to everything in that account. Why is this assumption wrong?
options: MCP servers only ever expose read-only resources, never actions
A server only exposes the specific tools and resources it was built to expose, further limited by whatever OAuth scopes were granted
Full account access is only granted on paid AI plans
MCP connections expire after a single session, limiting exposure automatically
auto-b3-mcp-explained.why: Assuming 'connected' means full account access is a listed common mistake — a server exposes only its specific built tools and resources, scoped further by the permissions granted during OAuth login.

auto-b3-mcp-explained.q: You're deciding whether to trust a local MCP server the same way you'd trust a remote hosted one. What's the correct distinction?
options: They carry identical risk since both use the same protocol
A local server runs with your own machine's permissions, while a remote server runs on someone else's infrastructure under granted access — different risk profiles
Local servers are always safer because they require no OAuth
Remote servers are always safer because they're maintained by vendors
auto-b3-mcp-explained.why: Treating local and remote servers as the same risk profile is a listed common mistake — a local server runs under your machine's own permissions, while a remote one runs on someone else's infrastructure under granted access.

auto-i1-connect-first-mcp-connector.q: You're connecting your first MCP connector and the settings offer both a read-only option and full read/write access, pre-selected as read/write. What should you do?
options: Leave the pre-selected read/write option since it's the default
Choose the narrower read-only scope for your first connection
Cancel the connection entirely rather than deal with scopes
Grant read/write but immediately revoke it after one test
auto-i1-connect-first-mcp-connector.why: Granting full read/write access by default because it's pre-selected, instead of checking for a narrower scope, is a listed common mistake — start with the narrowest scope offered.

auto-i1-connect-first-mcp-connector.q: Right after connecting a new MCP connector, you're tempted to immediately try a complex multi-step task. Why does the lesson advise a simple read-only test first?
options: Complex tasks are technically impossible until a read-only test has run once
If something goes wrong on a complex task first, you can't isolate whether the connector, the AI, or your instructions caused the failure
Read-only tests are required by the MCP protocol before any write action
It reduces the API cost of the first several tests
auto-i1-connect-first-mcp-connector.why: Skipping verification and immediately trying a complex multi-step task is a listed common mistake — if something goes wrong, you can't tell whether the connector, the AI, or your instructions caused it.

auto-i1-connect-first-mcp-connector.q: The read-only test prompt explicitly says "do not create, edit, or delete anything." Why include this constraint in a verification test?
options: It's required boilerplate with no functional effect
It isolates the test to confirm the connection works correctly without risking any unintended action while trust is still being built
It prevents the AI from reading any data at all
It's only needed for connectors that lack a read-only scope option
auto-i1-connect-first-mcp-connector.why: Explicitly forbidding write actions during the verification step matters most while you're still building trust in a brand-new connection and want to confirm behavior safely before granting more.

auto-i2-zapier-ai-automation.q: You write a ChatGPT Task's instructions around one hypothetical example instead of the real, messy input it will actually see each run. What happens?
options: ChatGPT automatically generalizes the instructions to handle any real input correctly
The first live run can behave differently than the test, since the task was never exercised against real data
The Task runs fine but only during manual Run Now tests
ChatGPT rejects the Task and refuses to schedule it
auto-i2-zapier-ai-automation.why: Writing the task's instructions around a single hypothetical example instead of the real input it will actually see each run is a listed common mistake — the first live run can behave differently than the test.

auto-i2-zapier-ai-automation.q: Your ChatGPT Task classifies leads and you need to scan the result in seconds every morning. Why does the instruction ask for a specific table format with fixed columns instead of open-ended prose?
options: Because ChatGPT Tasks technically cannot output prose
Because a specific, constrained format lets you act on the result reliably instead of parsing free-form text every run
Because it reduces the task's token cost to zero
Because ChatGPT Tasks cannot display tables in task history
auto-i2-zapier-ai-automation.why: Leaving the output format open-ended when you need a specific shape to act on makes the recurring output inconsistent from run to run — a constrained format prevents that.

auto-i2-zapier-ai-automation.q: You write a new ChatGPT Task, save it, and let the schedule fire for the first time without ever running it manually. What did the lesson recommend doing differently?
options: Nothing — the schedule firing once is sufficient before trusting it
Running it with Run Now against real data first, including checking how it handles the 'nothing new' case, before trusting the schedule
Waiting exactly 24 hours after creating it before letting the schedule fire
Skipping testing entirely since ChatGPT validates Tasks automatically
auto-i2-zapier-ai-automation.why: Turning on the schedule without running it manually against real data first, and without checking the 'nothing new' case, is a listed common mistake — Run Now testing surfaces problems before the first unattended run does.

auto-i3-n8n-make-workflow-ai-step.q: Your support-triage script needs to route messages to different log files based on an AI classification. Why should the headless `claude -p` call return valid JSON rather than a free-text sentence?
options: JSON is required by `claude -p` regardless of downstream needs
Structured JSON output is directly parseable by your script's branching logic without scraping free text
JSON outputs run faster than plain text outputs
Free-text outputs are not supported by Claude Code's headless mode
auto-i3-n8n-make-workflow-ai-step.why: Forcing structured JSON output makes the result directly parseable by your script's branching logic, without scraping a free-text sentence — critical when the next step branches on the value.

auto-i3-n8n-make-workflow-ai-step.q: You test your branching script only with typical, everyday support messages and skip testing the rare "complete outage" case that should trigger urgent escalation. What's the risk?
options: No risk — common-path testing is sufficient for any script
The rare branch remains unverified until it happens for real, exactly the scenario most testing misses
The script will refuse to run without testing every possible branch
Claude Code automatically generates edge-case tests for you
auto-i3-n8n-make-workflow-ai-step.why: Not testing the edge case that should hit the rare branch is a listed common mistake — most testing only exercises the common path, leaving the risky branch unverified until it happens live.

auto-i3-n8n-make-workflow-ai-step.q: Instead of parsing the AI step's JSON output and branching in code, you try to handle all decision-making inside one giant prompt passed to `claude -p`. What's the downside?
options: It makes the script cheaper to run
It makes the script harder to debug when only one branch misbehaves, since logic isn't separated into distinct, inspectable steps
Headless Claude Code calls cannot be used without a branching step
It automatically disables error handling in the rest of the script
auto-i3-n8n-make-workflow-ai-step.why: Skipping the branch-in-code step and doing all decision-making inside one giant AI prompt is a listed common mistake — it makes the script harder to debug when only one branch misbehaves.

auto-a1-design-safe-agent-instructions.q: An agent's instructions say "respond to customer emails professionally" with access to a send-email tool. What's the main safety gap here?
options: The instructions are too long and need to be shortened
The send action isn't explicitly constrained by a rule, so the agent could send external emails with no human check
The instructions don't mention which email provider to use
Professional tone can't be defined precisely enough for an AI to follow
auto-a1-design-safe-agent-instructions.why: Granting an agent a powerful action like send without a hard rule constraining it, assuming good judgment will suffice, is a listed common mistake — good judgment is not a substitute for an explicit boundary.

auto-a1-design-safe-agent-instructions.q: You write instructions covering the normal case but say nothing about what the agent should do when required information is missing or contradictory. What's the risk?
options: The agent will simply refuse to run at all
Agents default to improvising exactly where instructions don't specify, since writing only for the happy path leaves uncertainty undefined
Missing-information cases are automatically routed to a human by default in every platform
The instructions will fail validation before deployment
auto-a1-design-safe-agent-instructions.why: Writing instructions around the happy path only, with no rule for missing data or contradictions, is a listed common mistake — agents default to improvising exactly where you didn't specify.

auto-a1-design-safe-agent-instructions.q: After drafting agent instructions, you consider them finished. Why does the lesson insist on a red-team pass before deployment?
options: Red-teaming is only needed for agents with no tool access
Gaps in instructions are rarely visible to the person who wrote them, so a skeptical review surfaces unintended actions the author missed
It's a compliance requirement, not a practical safety step
It replaces the need for a human approval checkpoint
auto-a1-design-safe-agent-instructions.why: Treating instructions as done after the first draft instead of red-teaming them is a listed common mistake — the gaps are rarely visible to the person who wrote the instructions in the first place.

auto-a2-human-in-the-loop-error-handling.q: You add a Slack approval checkpoint before your automation sends refunds, but nobody is assigned to monitor that Slack channel. What's the practical result?
options: The automation will auto-approve after a timeout, so nothing changes
It becomes a silent backlog instead of an actual safety net
The Task or script automatically escalates unmonitored approvals to email
The checkpoint disables itself after 24 hours of inactivity
auto-a2-human-in-the-loop-error-handling.why: Building an approval checkpoint but never assigning or monitoring who responds to it is a listed common mistake — an approval checkpoint nobody monitors is worse than no checkpoint, since it becomes a silent backlog.

auto-a2-human-in-the-loop-error-handling.q: Your automation has an error path configured for malformed AI output, but you've only ever tested the happy path. What should you do before trusting it?
options: Nothing further, since the error path exists in the configuration
Deliberately break a step with bad credentials or malformed input to confirm the alert or approval path actually fires
Wait for a real production failure to validate it naturally
Remove the error path since untested paths add risk
auto-a2-human-in-the-loop-error-handling.why: Only testing the happy path, so an error path exists on paper but has never actually fired, is a listed common mistake — deliberately breaking a step confirms the alert or approval path works as designed.

auto-a2-human-in-the-loop-error-handling.q: A dependency your automation calls goes down, and your retry policy has no cap on retries. What's the likely consequence?
options: The automation will pause itself automatically until the dependency recovers
It can spam alerts or downstream systems, such as sending the same email multiple times, while the dependency is down
Nothing — uncapped retries are the safest default
The platform will automatically apply a cap regardless of configuration
auto-a2-human-in-the-loop-error-handling.why: Retrying failed steps indefinitely without a cap is a listed common mistake — it can spam alerts or downstream systems, like sending the same email multiple times, when a dependency is down.

auto-a3-cross-tool-pipeline.q: Your research-draft-publish pipeline's drafting stage has solid anti-hallucination instructions. Is it safe to wire the pipeline straight to auto-publish without a human review step?
options: Yes, strong anti-hallucination instructions are a sufficient safeguard on their own
No — those instructions reduce but don't eliminate errors, so a human review step before publishing is still required
Yes, as long as the research stage uses a research-capable AI like Gemini Deep Research
No, but only because publishing pipelines legally require human sign-off
auto-a3-cross-tool-pipeline.why: Skipping the human review stage and wiring the pipeline straight to publish, assuming anti-hallucination instructions alone are sufficient, is a listed common mistake — they reduce but don't eliminate errors.

auto-a3-cross-tool-pipeline.q: The drafting-stage prompt omits the instruction to use only the supplied research findings. What's the likely failure mode?
options: The draft will simply be shorter than requested
The draft can blend real research with invented-sounding filler that's hard to tell apart on a quick read
The pipeline will fail to run entirely
The publish step will automatically reject the draft
auto-a3-cross-tool-pipeline.why: Letting the drafting stage's prompt omit the 'use only supplied research' constraint is a listed common mistake — it lets the draft blend real research with invented-sounding filler that's hard to catch on a quick read.

auto-a3-cross-tool-pipeline.q: You trust a polished-looking draft without checking the research stage's raw output first. Why is this risky?
options: Polished drafts are always accurate regardless of source quality
If the research stage returned thin or off-topic findings, the draft will look polished but be built on weak material
The draft stage always flags weak research automatically in bold text
It's not risky as long as a human eventually reviews the final draft
auto-a3-cross-tool-pipeline.why: Not inspecting the research stage's raw output before trusting the draft is a listed common mistake — thin or off-topic findings can still produce a draft that looks polished but rests on weak material.

auto-a4-evaluate-maintain-automations.q: An automation has been running without any errors for months, so the team assumes it's working correctly. What's the flaw in this assumption?
options: Automations without errors are always working correctly by definition
An automation can run without erroring while quietly producing wrong output that never trips an error path
Zero errors means the automation platform is being underused
It should have been retired regardless of error rate after six months
auto-a4-evaluate-maintain-automations.why: Treating 'it's still running' as equivalent to 'it's still working correctly' is a listed common mistake — an AI step can produce technically valid but subtly wrong output, like a bad classification, without ever tripping an error path.

auto-a4-evaluate-maintain-automations.q: A run log shows 140 runs with 6 errors all containing the message "invalid_grant." What does this pattern most likely indicate, and what should you check first?
options: A rate limit issue — check the API provider's usage dashboard
An expired or revoked OAuth token on a connected account — check connector status in the platform's settings
A data format change — check the trigger app's field mappings
AI output drift — check the model version being used
auto-a4-evaluate-maintain-automations.why: The repeated 'invalid_grant' error message strongly suggests an expired or revoked OAuth token on a connected account, and the diagnostic prompt is designed to point you to checking connector status first rather than guessing.

auto-a4-evaluate-maintain-automations.q: No single person is assigned to review any of the team's automations, though several people know they exist. What's the practical consequence?
options: The automations will automatically flag themselves for review when needed
An automation everyone assumes someone else is watching is an automation nobody is actually watching
This has no consequence as long as error rates stay at zero
Automation platforms require an assigned owner before they can run at all
auto-a4-evaluate-maintain-automations.why: Letting automations accumulate with no single owner responsible for reviewing each one is a listed common mistake — an automation everyone assumes someone else is watching is an automation nobody is watching.
